newsitem.title: CANADA: Canadian T-bills open weaker ahead of auction.
newsitem.headline: Canadian T-bills open weaker ahead of auction.

text.p: Canadian T-bills opened softer on Wednesday ahead of the weekly auction with a softer dollar, weak U.S. market, and lack of buying from domestic accounts weighing on prices, dealers said.

"It's a combination of things. Obviously U.S. Treasury prices are a little bit weaker here, which isn't helping. The Canadian dollar is looking a little shaky again," said one dealer with a bank-owned brokerage. "I think more than anything it's apathy on the part of domestic accounts."
Canada's three-month when-issued T-bill softened to yield 2.88 percent from 2.86 percent at Tuesday's close.
Dealers have commented for several sessions on the lack of buying interest by accounts, citing a lack of incentive given the recent decline in T-bill yields and risk of higher rates.

"We've got an auction to deal with here today, so with the supply coming on the market just needs to cheapen up a little bit to garner some interest," the dealer said. "The risk/reward in (accounts') minds is not for lower rates."

The Bank of Canada this afternoon will auction C$4.5 billion of three-month, six-month and one-year bills. The auction was delayed until today because of yesterday's St Jean Baptiste Day public and market holiday in Quebec.
In other prices, the six-month when-issued T-bill softened to yield 3.18 percent from 3.16 percent. The one-year T-bill firmed to yield 3.67 percent from 3.64 percent.
The call loan or overnight lending rate traded at 2.95 percent, near the middle of the Bank of Canada's 2.75-3.25 percent target range.
The Bank of Canada's monetary conditions index was trading at a record low of -6.26, according to Reuters calculations.
